title: Mitotic figures require a polarised force like magnetism, not mechanical traction

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Mitotic figures require a polarised force like magnetism, not mechanical traction

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: The spindle and asters of dividing cells are lines of force of a bipolar field made visible by more permeable particles, like iron filings between magnet poles, and they cannot be explained by mere mechanical traction on a protoplasmic web but require some polarised and polarising force analogous to magnetism or electricity.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. IV: On the Internal Form and Structure of the Cell

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: any explanation which is based, like Rhumbler’s, on mere mechanical traction, is obviously inadequate, and we shall find ourselves limited to the hypothesis of some polarised and polarising force, such as we deal with, for instance, in the phenomena of magnetism or electricity.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter IV, “On the Internal Form and Structure of the Cell”; topic “Spindle and asters as lines of force”. Scope: caryokinetic (mitotic) division of animal and plant cells

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch04-02: resolvable-now, resolvability 0.71

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The categorical rejection of traction has clear observable consequences, and open perturbation microscopy can test whether microtubule mechanics account for spindle behavior. The unspecified nature of the alternative polarizing field lowers operationalizability but does not prevent refuting the claim.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Use live-cell spindle imaging and perturbation data to test whether spindle fibers transmit mechanical traction and whether a distinct magnetism-like bipolar field is needed to predict chromosome and particle motion. Evidence of tensile microtubule forces sufficient to explain the pattern refutes the exclusion of mechanical traction.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Images alone may not directly measure force.

The proposed field is analogical rather than quantitatively specified.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Images and perturbation screens can test the part of the claim that denies a mechanical explanation and requires a field force of the magnetic kind. That is a proxy for Thompson's analogy rather than a direct measurement of a magnetic body force, which lowers operationalizability. The mechanical account is discriminable where motors and microtubules are perturbed, and those experiments are public for a limited set of cells.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Ask whether spindle and aster geometry persists when microtubule mechanics and motor traction are removed, and whether a magnetic-like body force is required to keep the figure. Collapse of the figure under mechanical disruption, with no need for a magnetic or electric body force, would refute the claim; a figure that survives loss of traction and tracks an applied polarised field would support it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Reading 'polarised force' as microtubule polarity is a modern gloss on a magnetic or electric analogy.

Force-ablation measurements are sparser in repositories than the images of the figure.

Repository coverage is model cell types, not every animal and plant mitosis.
